findings.title: Validator accepts quoted string 'false' that the loader treats as allowing implicit invocation
findings.evidence: The new check is String(config.policy?.allow_implicit_invocation)==='false'. That passes for both boolean false and the string "false", which parseYaml returns for a quoted scalar such as allow_implicit_invocation: "false". The loader only disables implicit invocation for boolean false and treats every other value as allowing it. So a config the validator approves as human-only still gets implicit invocation at load time. That breaks the spec and bypasses the authorization control. The old strict check (===false) rejected this case correctly.

findings.title: Validator now approves string 'false', but the loader treats that value as allowing implicit invocation
findings.evidence: Spec: approve only when the loader will disable implicit invocation, and the loader requires boolean false. Context: parseYaml returns a string for a quoted scalar (allow_implicit_invocation: "false" -> 'false'), and the loader treats every value except boolean false as allowing implicit invocation. The new check String(v)==='false' is true for both boolean false and the string 'false'. So a config with a quoted value passes as human-only while the loader still allows implicit invocation. The old check (===false) rejected it correctly. This breaks the validator's contract with the loader and is a security problem.

findings.title: Validator approves quoted string 'false', but the loader treats it as allowing implicit invocation
findings.evidence: Both the Security and Data & contracts lenses reported this; merged here. The new check is String(config.policy?.allow_implicit_invocation)==='false'. It is true for boolean false and also for the string 'false'. parseYaml returns the string 'false' for a quoted scalar such as allow_implicit_invocation: "false". The loader disables implicit invocation only for boolean false and treats every other value as allowing it. So the validator approves such a config as human-only while the loader still allows implicit invocation. This breaks the spec ('approve only when the loader will disable implicit invocation; the loader requires a boolean false value') and the validator's contract with the loader, and it bypasses the authorization control. The old check (===false) correctly rejected this input.

findings.title: Install now deletes real directories/files at the target, which loses user data and has no way to roll back
findings.evidence: The old code kept the guard `if(fs[target] && fs[target].kind!=='link') return false;`. The new code removes it and runs `delete fs[target];` without any condition, then assigns a link node. The context says directory nodes can hold user-created content, that assignment replaces the whole node, and that callers keep no backup. So any existing directory or file at the target is destroyed for good. This breaks the spec's requirement to keep real directories and files and return false on those conflicts. The function now always returns true.
findings.location: module.js: install(), `delete fs[target];` line (guard check removed)

findings.title: Save control no longer activates with Enter or Space
findings.evidence: The old version rendered a native <button> ({tag:'button',type:'button',...}). The new version renders {tag:'div',role:'button',tabIndex:0,onClick:save}. findings.title: Removing `name` from the response breaks installed mobile clients that still use it
findings.evidence: The spec says to add displayName while still supporting installed clients that read `name`, and says every consumer must keep rendering a label. Mobile releases stay active for 90 days, and legacy code calls payload.name.toUpperCase(). Before the change, the response returned {id, name, displayName}. After it, the response returns only {id, displayName}. On older clients payload.name is now undefined, so payload.name.toUpperCase() throws a TypeError and no label renders. Fix: keep `name: row.name` next to `displayName` until the 90-day window has passed with no remaining legacy readers, then remove it in a planned deprecation.

No contract or schema tests for the response shape were provided to check that both fields are present.

findings.title: Tenant check now trusts request.tenant from the URL instead of session.tenant, so any caller can read documents from other tenants
findings.evidence: The spec says to return a document only to a session from the document's tenant, and it says request tenant filters are untrusted. The context says find(id) is a global lookup with no tenant scoping and that request parameters come straight from the URL. The before code compared row.tenant === session.tenant. The after code compares row.tenant === request.tenant. Because the caller controls both request.id and request.tenant, they can set tenant to match any document's tenant and get that document back. This is a cross-tenant data leak, and the verified session identity is no longer used in the check.

findings.title: Tenant authorization check now trusts the request's tenant parameter instead of the verified session tenant
findings.evidence: The check changed from `row.tenant === session.tenant` to `row.tenant === request.tenant`. find(id) looks up documents globally with no tenant scoping, and request parameters come straight from the URL. An attacker from any tenant can send ?id=<victim doc>&tenant=<victim tenant> and get back another tenant's document. This breaks the spec: return a document only to a session from the document's tenant, and treat request tenant filters as untrusted. It is a cross-tenant IDOR/broken access control.

findings.title: Put permission widened from releases/ prefix to entire assets bucket
findings.evidence: The spec says the deployment identity may write only object keys under releases/. The before resource was 'assets/releases/*'. The after resource is 'assets/*'. The evaluator treats a trailing * as matching any suffix, so the identity can now run object:Put on any key in the assets bucket. That breaks least privilege. It also widens the blast radius: a compromised or buggy deploy could overwrite or plant objects anywhere in the bucket, outside releases/.

findings.title: Prune predicate widened from exact managed-link match to prefix match, so aliases and links to files inside a skill get deleted
findings.evidence: The spec says a managed link must point exactly to /repo/skills/<name>, and that aliases and links to files within a skill must be kept. The 'before' code checked target==='/repo/skills/'+name. The 'after' code checks target.startsWith('/repo/skills/'). Any entry not in live whose target is under /repo/skills/ now gets returned. That includes an alias (for example installed/foo -> /repo/skills/bar) and a link to a file inside a skill (for example installed/x -> /repo/skills/bar/file.md). The caller unlinks every returned name, so user-created links are destroyed. This widens the blast radius of a destructive operation and breaks the spec's contract.

findings.title: Prefix check has no path-boundary or normalization guard
findings.evidence: startsWith('/repo/skills/') also matches targets like '/repo/skills/../other' and any deeper path. Nothing confirms the target is exactly one path segment that equals the installation name. Without that check, removals can reach links outside the managed set.

gaps: No tests show how aliases or nested-file links are handled before and after the change
No dry-run or rollback path for the caller's unlink step could be checked from the supplied evidence

That includes aliases such as {foo: '/repo/skills/bar'} and file links such as {x: '/repo/skills/bar/file.md'}. gaps: The change includes no tests. There is no coverage for aliases, file links inside a skill, or exact-match managed links.
Not checked: whether the names in entries or live can contain path separators or need normalising (for example, trailing slashes).

findings.title: Stale-response guard removed: older responses can overwrite results for the newest query
findings.evidence: The before version saved `const request=++state.request` and the callback returned early when `request!==state.request`, so only the latest request could write `state.items`. The after version still increments `state.request` but never captures or compares it, and the callback assigns `state.items=items` unconditionally. The context says fetchResults does not guarantee callback order. So if a user types 'a' and then 'ab', and the 'a' response arrives last, the screen shows results for 'a'. This breaks the spec: 'must display results for the most recently entered query. Older in-flight responses may arrive after newer ones.'

gaps: The change includes no tests. Nothing covers responses arriving out of order, such as the older query's callback firing after the newer one's.

The context says fetchResults does not guarantee callback order, and the spec says older in-flight responses may arrive after newer ones. So a slow response for an earlier query can replace the results for the latest query. The user then sees results that don't match what they typed, which breaks the spec requirement to display results for the most recently entered query.

findings.title: The /repo guard checks only one alias hop, but the write uses the full chain, so writes can escape into /repo
findings.evidence: The change replaced `const resolved=canonical(path,links)` with `const resolved=links[path] || path`. The guard now looks only at the first alias hop. `operations.push(canonical(path,links)+'/tool')` still follows the complete chain. Example: with links {'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}, install('/a') checks '/b', which passes the guard, and then records '/repo/x/tool'. This breaks the spec rule to refuse any destination that resolves anywhere within /repo before recording an operation. The protection boundary no longer holds, so the change widens the blast radius into the protected tree. The fix is to restore `canonical()` for the check and reuse `resolved` in the push.

findings.title: Guard checks only one alias hop, so multi-hop chains into /repo slip through

The write still goes to `canonical(path,links)+'/tool'`, which follows the whole chain. Example: links={'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}. Here resolved='/b' passes the check, then operations gets '/repo/x/tool'. The spec says to refuse any destination that resolves within /repo before an operation is recorded, so this reintroduces a write into /repo. The value that is checked and the value that is used are now computed differently.

Fix: go back to `resolved=canonical(path,links)`, use `resolved` in the push, and add tests for 0, 1 and 2+ hop chains plus the exact '/repo' boundary.

gaps: No test files were supplied, so I couldn't confirm what existing tests cover.
I assumed `links` has no cycles; `canonical` would loop forever on a cyclic map, and that issue was already there before this change.

findings.title: Transaction boundary removed; a rejected credit leaves the debit committed (data loss / broken atomicity)
findings.evidence: The spec says: 'A rejected debit must leave both balances unchanged. Use the supplied transaction boundary so all writes commit together.' According to the context, db.save writes immediately and throws for a frozen destination account. The after code calls db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount) outside db.transaction, so that debit is persisted at once. When the next db.save(to, ...) throws because the destination is frozen, the source has already lost `amount` and the destination never receives it, so the money is gone. The before code wrapped both writes in db.transaction(tx => ...), which commits only if the callback returns.
findings.location: module.js transfer(): lines `db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount);` and `db.save(to, db.get(to)+amount);` (removed `return db.transaction(tx => {...})`)

findings.title: Reads moved outside the snapshot and the transaction result is no longer returned
findings.evidence: The before code read balances with tx.get inside an isolated snapshot and returned the result of db.transaction. The after code reads with db.get outside any isolation, so concurrent transfers can read the same balance and overwrite each other's update. It also returns undefined, which breaks any caller that used the transaction's return value.

gaps: The change includes no tests. Nothing checks that a frozen destination (save throws) leaves both balances unchanged, or that a successful transfer commits both writes together.
I could not confirm whether any callers use transfer()'s return value.

findings.title: Retrying after a partial failure debits the source again
findings.evidence: Because the debit is committed before the credit can fail, a caller or operator who retries a failed transfer debits the source a second time. The operation is therefore not idempotent. On-call cannot tell a failure with no writes from a failure with half the writes done, because the thrown error carries no transfer context and no record of the debit already applied. Fixing it means reconciling balances by hand. The original transaction made a failure all-or-nothing, so a retry was safe.
findings.location: module.js: transfer(), the sequence of two non-transactional db.save calls

findings.title: Transfer result is no longer returned to callers

gaps: The return type of db.transaction (for example, a promise or a value) isn't specified, so the impact of dropping the return value is inferred.

findings.title: Put permission widened from releases/ prefix to entire assets bucket
findings.evidence: Spec: deployment identity may write only object keys under releases/ in the assets bucket. Before: resource 'assets/releases/*'. After: resource 'assets/*'. The evaluator treats a trailing * as matching any suffix, so 'assets/*' now allows object:Put on any key in the bucket (e.g. assets/index.html, assets/config/...). This breaks least privilege, and a compromised or buggy deploy could overwrite or corrupt any object in the bucket, not just release artifacts.

The spec says a managed link is one where /installed/<name> points exactly to /repo/skills/<name>, and that aliases and links to files inside a skill must be kept. The old predicate `target==='/repo/skills/'+name` enforced this. The new predicate `!live.includes(name) && target.startsWith('/repo/skills/')` returns every non-live entry whose target is anywhere under the skills root. Examples: the alias `foo-alias` -> `/repo/skills/foo` and the file link `x` -> `/repo/skills/foo/bin/x`. The context says the caller unlinks every name that prune returns, so links the spec says to keep get deleted. Fix: restore the exact-match check `target==='/repo/skills/'+name`.

findings.title: Validation accepts allow_implicit_invocation:false from any top-level section, bypassing the human-only policy
findings.evidence: The new code `Object.values(config).some(section => section?.allow_implicit_invocation===false)` passes if any top-level section sets the flag to false. The loader only reads `config.policy.allow_implicit_invocation`, and a missing policy defaults to allowing implicit invocation. So a config like `{other:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}}`, or one with `policy.allow_implicit_invocation:true` plus `other.allow_implicit_invocation:false`, passes validation. The tool is still loaded as implicitly invocable. This breaks the spec, which requires the flag to be false under the root `policy` key, and it turns a default-deny check into a bypass.

findings.title: Validation now accepts allow_implicit_invocation:false under any top-level section, not just policy, which breaks the loader contract
findings.evidence: The spec says validation passes only when policy.allow_implicit_invocation is false at the document root. The loader reads only config.policy.allow_implicit_invocation, and a missing policy permits implicit invocation. The new code returns true when any top-level value has allow_implicit_invocation===false. Example: {metadata:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}} with no policy now passes validation, but the loader treats the tool as implicitly invocable. Example: {policy:{allow_implicit_invocation:true}, other:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}} also passes. In both cases a tool meant to be human-only can be invoked implicitly. This is a security and contract break. The old check, config.policy?.allow_implicit_invocation===false, was correct.

gaps: No tests were supplied to confirm which config shapes are rejected.

findings.title: Removing `name` from the response breaks installed mobile clients that still read it
findings.evidence: The spec requires support for installed clients that still read `name`, and says every consumer must keep rendering a label. Mobile releases stay active for 90 days, and legacy code calls `payload.name.toUpperCase()`. Before the change, the response included `name:row.name`. After it, the response is only `{id:row.id, displayName:row.name}`. So `payload.name` is undefined, and `undefined.toUpperCase()` throws a TypeError. Legacy clients will crash or show no label. Keep `name:row.name` next to `displayName` until the 90-day mobile support window has passed.

findings.title: Idempotency key changed from event.id to attemptId, so retries cause duplicate charges
findings.evidence: The change replaces `return charge(event.id);` with `return charge(attemptId);`. According to the context, charge(key) deduplicates only on equal keys, and each retry gets a new attemptId while event.id stays the same. Each retried delivery, including one after a worker restart, will send a new key and create a second charge. This breaks the spec: 'A retried delivery of the same event must not create a second charge, including after a worker restarts.' Because each duplicate charge has a valid, distinct key, the provider reports no conflict. On-call has no signal to detect the duplicates, and fixing them means reconciling and refunding customers by hand. Fix: go back to charge(event.id), or another key that stays the same across retries and restarts.

gaps: No tests or retry/restart scenarios were provided to show duplicate-charge behavior end to end.
Logging and metrics around deliver() were not provided, so I couldn't check whether duplicate charges would be detectable.

findings.title: Escape no longer restores focus to the opening control
findings.evidence: Spec: "Closing the dialog with Escape must restore focus to the same control that opened it." Before: onKey sets state.open=false and then calls state.trigger.focus(). After: onKey sets state.open=false and the trigger.focus() call is removed. The context says the renderer unmounts the dialog when state.open is false and that trigger.focus() is the available way to restore focus. With the call removed, focus is left on the unmounted dialog content and falls back to document.body, so keyboard and screen reader users lose their place in the page.

findings.title: Tenant authorization trusts the URL-supplied request.tenant instead of the verified session.tenant, allowing cross-tenant document reads (IDOR)
findings.evidence: The Security and Staff engineer reports found the same defect, so they are merged here. Before the change, read() returned the row only when `row.tenant === session.tenant`, so access depended on the session identity verified upstream. After the change, it checks `row.tenant === request.tenant`. The context says request parameters come directly from the URL and that find(id) is a global lookup with no tenant scoping. A caller from any tenant can therefore supply a document id and set `tenant` to that document's tenant, and read() will return the row. This breaks the spec: 'Return a document only to a session from the document tenant. Request tenant filters are untrusted.' Fix: compare against session.tenant again.
findings.location: module.js: read(), return statement `return row && row.tenant === request.tenant ? row : null;`

gaps: I removed the Staff engineer's should-fix finding about missing tests and recorded it here as a gap. Missing tests are not a defect introduced by this change. Tests should still cover these cases: a matching session tenant returns the row, a different session tenant returns null, and a spoofed request.tenant returns null.
No test files or callers were supplied, so I could not check whether any caller relies on request.tenant.
I took session.tenant as always present and trustworthy, as the context states, and did not verify this.

findings.title: /repo guard checks only one link hop, so multi-hop aliases into /repo get through
findings.evidence: The new code sets `const resolved=links[path] || path;`, which follows only one link. The old code used `canonical(path,links)`, which follows the whole chain. The write target is still `canonical(path,links)+'/tool'`. So the path that gets checked is not the path that gets written. Example: with links {'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}, install('/a') sets resolved to '/b', the check passes, and the code records '/repo/x/tool'. That breaks the spec ('refuse a link destination that resolves anywhere within /repo') and allows writes into the protected repo tree.

gaps: Nothing was run, so the multi-hop bypass is shown by tracing the code by hand, not by a test.
No tests cover link chains of two or more hops. The brief doesn't show whether such tests exist.

findings.title: Repo containment check only resolves one alias hop, so multi-hop chains into /repo get past it
findings.evidence: After the change, the check uses `const resolved=links[path] || path;`, which follows only one link. The write still goes to `canonical(path,links)+'/tool'`, which follows the whole chain. Example: links={'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}. Here resolved='/b' passes the check, but the code records the operation '/repo/x/tool'. That breaks the spec: a destination that resolves anywhere inside /repo must be refused. The old code checked the same fully resolved path it wrote to. This is a regression and a security hole, because writes can land inside /repo.

findings.title: The path that gets checked is resolved differently from the path that gets written
findings.evidence: The check uses a one-hop lookup and the write calls canonical() again, so the two can disagree. Resolve the path once with canonical() and use that single value for both the check and the push: `const resolved=canonical(path,links); ... operations.push(resolved+'/tool')`.

gaps: The change includes no tests. Nothing covers a multi-hop alias chain that ends inside /repo, or a chain that ends at /repo itself.

findings.title: The /repo guard follows only one link hop, but the write uses the fully resolved path, so multi-hop aliases into /repo get through
findings.evidence: Before the change, install() set resolved=canonical(path,links), which follows the whole link chain. The guard therefore checked the same path that was written. After the change, it sets `const resolved=links[path] || path;`, which follows only one hop. The write is still `operations.push(canonical(path,links)+'/tool')`. Trace: with links={'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}, install('/a',...) gets resolved='/b'. That value passes both the `=== '/repo'` and `startsWith('/repo/')` checks, so '/repo/x/tool' is recorded and true is returned. A chain ending at '/repo' itself (for example '/a'->'/b'->'/repo') records '/repo/tool' the same way. This breaks the spec, which says to refuse any destination that resolves anywhere within /repo before an operation is recorded. It also lets writes into the protected tree, and it is a regression from the old code. Both the Infrastructure and Staff engineer reports raised this as a blocker. The Staff engineer report filed a second should-fix, 'The path that gets checked is resolved differently from the path that gets written'. It has the same root cause, so it is merged here as the fix: resolve the path once with canonical() and use that one value for both the check and the push (`const resolved=canonical(path,links); ... operations.push(resolved+'/tool')`).
findings.location: module.js install(): `const resolved=links[path] || path;` (and the inconsistent `operations.push(canonical(path,links)+'/tool')`)

gaps: Nothing was run. The multi-hop bypass was shown by tracing the code by hand, not by a test.
The change includes no tests for link chains of two or more hops that end inside /repo or at /repo itself. The brief doesn't show whether such tests already exist.

findings.title: Transaction boundary removed; a rejected credit leaves the debit committed (data loss)
findings.evidence: The after code calls db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount) and then db.save(to, ...) directly. Per the context, db.save writes immediately and throws for a frozen destination account. If `to` is frozen, the debit to `from` is already persisted when the second save throws, so funds vanish. This violates the spec: 'A rejected debit must leave both balances unchanged. Use the supplied transaction boundary so all writes commit together.' The before code wrapped both writes in db.transaction(tx => ...), which only commits if the callback returns.
findings.location: module.js: transfer, lines 2-3 (db.save calls replacing the tx.save calls inside db.transaction)

findings.title: Return value of transfer changed from the transaction result to undefined
findings.evidence: Before: `return db.transaction(...)` passed the transaction result to callers. After: transfer has no return statement, so callers that relied on the result, or awaited it if transaction is async, now get undefined.

findings.title: Reads moved outside the isolated snapshot
findings.evidence: db.get is now read outside any transaction, so the read-modify-write is not isolated. Concurrent transfers can interleave and lose updates. The before code read through tx.get inside the snapshot.

gaps: No tests were supplied. I couldn't check for a test that makes the destination save throw (frozen account) and then asserts both balances are unchanged.
I couldn't confirm whether db.transaction is sync or async, so how much the dropped return value affects callers is unknown.

findings.title: Transaction boundary removed: a failed credit leaves the debit committed, so money is lost
findings.evidence: The spec says a rejected debit must leave both balances unchanged and all writes must commit together. The context says db.save writes immediately and throws when the destination account is frozen. In the new code, db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount) runs first and persists right away. If db.save(to, ...) then throws because the destination is frozen, the source has already been debited and the destination was never credited. Nothing rolls this back. The old code put both writes inside db.transaction, which commits only if the callback returns, so the same failure left both balances unchanged.
findings.location: module.js transfer(): lines `db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount);` and `db.save(to, db.get(to)+amount);` (db.transaction wrapper removed)

findings.title: Reads and writes are no longer isolated, so concurrent transfers can overwrite each other
findings.evidence: The new code reads with db.get and writes with db.save directly, outside the isolated snapshot that db.transaction provides. If two transfers run at the same time, both can read the same old balance and the second write overwrites the first, so one update is lost.

findings.title: transfer() no longer returns the transaction result
findings.evidence: The old code returned db.transaction(...), so callers got back the transaction's result (for example a promise or a commit status). The new code returns undefined. Any caller that awaits or checks that value will now silently get nothing back.

gaps: The context doesn't say whether db.transaction returns a value or a promise, or what it returns, so I can't confirm how much the lost return value affects callers.

findings.title: Retrying a failed transfer debits the source account again

If a caller or on-call engineer retries the transfer, it subtracts the amount again. On-call also can't spot or fix the inconsistency without rebuilding balances by hand. With the old transaction, a failure committed nothing, so retrying was safe.

findings.title: Monthly checkout now says the price is "Then $12/year" instead of "Then $12/month"
findings.evidence: The spec says the monthly checkout must show "Then $12/month" before checkout. The context confirms this is the monthly plan, charged after seven days, and that action.note is shown to the user before they submit. The change replaces note:'Then $12/month' with note:'Then $12/year'. Users would see the wrong billing period and expect to pay $12 a year, but they would be charged $12 a month. This breaks the spec and gives users misleading pricing at checkout. The annual plan has its own screen, so this copy isn't meant for it.

findings.title: Selection stored as index archives the wrong row after filter or sort
findings.evidence: select now returns the row index, and the parent keeps that selection when filter and sort replace the rows. archiveSelected then reads rows[selection].id from the new array, so the index can point to a different row. The archive callback then persists the wrong id. This breaks the spec that archive acts on the row the user selected. The change replaces a stable, unique, immutable id with a positional index. If the new list is shorter, rows[selection] is undefined and the code throws a TypeError.

findings.title: No tests cover archiving after filter or reorder, or an out-of-range selection
findings.evidence: The spec's key behavior is that archive stays correct after filter or sort. The change includes no tests for that case, nor for a selection index that is out of range or has no matching row. A regression test would have caught the bug above.

gaps: The parent state and the filter/sort code were not supplied. The preserved-selection behavior is taken from the brief's context.
No tests were supplied, so I could not tell whether any existing tests exercise this path.

findings.title: Archive acts on wrong row after filter/sort because selection is now a positional index
findings.evidence: Spec requires archive to act on the user-selected row even after the list is filtered or reordered. Context says filter and sort replace rows but preserve selection in parent state. The change makes select return an index and archiveSelected resolve rows[selection].id at archive time, so the preserved index points at whatever row now occupies that position. This can archive a different record, or throw if the index is out of range. The before code stored the immutable id, which was stable across reordering. The change introduces the defect and breaks the spec.

gaps: No tests or UI code were supplied to show how the parent state consumes the selection value. Any other consumer of select()'s return value may also be affected by the id-to-index change.

findings.title: Selection is now stored as a row index, so archive hits the wrong row after a filter or sort
findings.evidence: Both the Staff engineer and Product reports found this. Before the change, select returned rows[index].id, which is immutable and unique. After the change, `select(rows,index) { return index; }` returns the position instead. Per the context, the parent state keeps this selection when filter or sort replaces rows. archiveSelected then runs `archive(rows[selection].id)` on the new array. That index can point to a different row, so archive saves the wrong id. This breaks the spec requirement that archive act on the row the user selected. If the new list is shorter than the index, rows[selection] is undefined and accessing .id throws a TypeError. Either way, data is changed by mistake or the user sees a failure.

gaps: I removed the Staff engineer finding about missing tests (should-fix). It points to coverage that isn't there, not a defect introduced by this change. The core regression is covered by the merged blocker.
The Product report raised a possible risk: other code that reads select()'s return value might also be affected by the switch from id to index. No such code was supplied, so I couldn't confirm it.

findings.title: Retry-specific idempotency key permits duplicate charges
findings.evidence: The change replaces event.id with attemptId as the provider idempotency key. Retries retain event.id but receive a new attemptId, so the provider can create a second charge for the same event, including after a worker restart. This violates the required retry contract.

findings.title: Preserve the event ID as the charge idempotency key

findings.title: Put permission widened from releases/ prefix to entire assets bucket (least-privilege violation)
findings.evidence: Before: resource:'assets/releases/*' limited object:Put to keys under releases/. After: resource:'assets/*'. The evaluator treats a trailing * as matching any suffix, so the deployment identity can now write any object key in the assets bucket. The spec says it may write only object keys under releases/. This breaks the access contract and widens the blast radius: a compromised or buggy deploy could overwrite or plant any asset in the bucket.
findings.location: module.js: policy() return value, resource field

The evaluator treats a trailing * as matching any suffix, so object:Put now matches every key in the assets bucket, not just releases/. That lets the identity overwrite or plant any asset in the bucket, which breaks least privilege and the spec's contract.

findings.title: Deployment identity's object:Put now covers the whole assets bucket, not just releases/

The context says statements go to the evaluator unchanged, and its prefix matcher treats a trailing * as matching any suffix. So object:Put now matches every key in the assets bucket, which lets the identity overwrite or add objects outside releases/. This breaks the spec and least privilege. findings.title: Removed stale-response guard lets older queries overwrite newer results
findings.evidence: Before: `const request=++state.request;` was captured, and the callback did `if(request!==state.request) return;` so only the latest request could write state.items. After: `++state.request;` is not captured, and the callback always runs `state.items=items;`. The context says fetchResults does not guarantee callback order, and the spec says older responses may arrive after newer ones. So if a response for an earlier query arrives late, it overwrites state.items and the screen shows results for a query that is no longer current. This breaks the spec requirement to show results for the most recently entered query. The counter is still incremented, but nothing reads it now.

findings.title: Guard only resolves one link hop, so multi-hop aliases can write into /repo

findings.title: Idempotency key changed from event.id to attemptId, so every retry creates a duplicate charge
findings.evidence: The context says charge(key) is the provider's idempotency API, where equal keys return the existing charge, and that a retry reuses event.id but gets a new attemptId. Before the change, deliver called charge(event.id), so retries, including those after a worker restart, landed on the existing charge. After the change, deliver calls charge(attemptId). Each retry now sends a new key, and the provider creates a new charge. This breaks the spec: 'A retried delivery of the same event must not create a second charge, including after a worker restarts.' findings.title: Tenant authorization check now trusts the request's tenant value instead of the session's tenant, so any user can read any tenant's documents
findings.evidence: The spec says to return a document only to a session from the document's tenant, and that request tenant filters are untrusted. The context says find(id) is a global lookup with no tenant scoping, and request parameters come straight from the URL. The before code checked `row.tenant === session.tenant`. The after code checks `row.tenant === request.tenant`. An attacker can set ?id=<victim doc>&tenant=<victim tenant> and get the document back, even though their verified session belongs to a different tenant. This breaks server-side authorization and exposes data across tenants.
findings.location: module.js:read, line 3 (`return row && row.tenant === request.tenant ? row : null;`)

findings.title: Tenant authorization now checks the untrusted request.tenant instead of session.tenant, so any user can read any tenant's documents
findings.evidence: Both the Security and Staff engineer reports found this. The spec says to return a document only to a session from the document's tenant, and that request tenant filters are untrusted. The context says find(id) is a global lookup with no tenant scoping, and that request parameters come straight from the URL. Before the change, the code checked `row.tenant === session.tenant`, which uses the session identity verified upstream. After the change, it checks `row.tenant === request.tenant`. An attacker can send ?id=<victim doc>&tenant=<victim tenant> and get the row back, whatever tenant their session belongs to. This leaks data across tenants and breaks the authorization contract. The fix is to restore the comparison against session.tenant.
findings.location: module.js:read, line 3 (`return row && row.tenant === request.tenant ? row : null;`)

gaps: I dropped the Staff engineer finding about missing regression tests. It isn't a defect in the code under review, and no test files were supplied, so I couldn't confirm whether existing tests cover the tenant check. A regression test is still worth adding: when session.tenant !== row.tenant, read should return null, whether request.tenant matches the row or is missing.

findings.title: Validation accepts allow_implicit_invocation:false from any top-level section, not just policy
findings.evidence: The spec says validation passes only if policy.allow_implicit_invocation is boolean false at the document root. The new code checks Object.values(config).some(section => section?.allow_implicit_invocation===false), so a config like {metadata:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}} with no policy (or with policy.allow_implicit_invocation:true) passes. The loader reads only config.policy.allow_implicit_invocation, and a missing policy defaults to permitting implicit invocation. So a tool can pass validation as human-only while the loader still lets it be invoked implicitly. That bypasses the authorization control and breaks default-deny.

findings.title: Validation now accepts allow_implicit_invocation:false from any top-level section, not just policy
findings.evidence: The spec says validation should pass only when policy.allow_implicit_invocation is boolean false. The old code checked exactly that: `config.policy?.allow_implicit_invocation===false`. The new code uses `Object.values(config).some(section => section?.allow_implicit_invocation===false)`, which passes when any top-level section sets the flag to false. For example, `{metadata:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}}` with no policy now passes. The same is true for `{policy:{allow_implicit_invocation:true}, other:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}}`. The loader reads only config.policy.allow_implicit_invocation and permits implicit invocation when policy is missing. So a tool can pass as human-only while the loader still lets it be invoked implicitly. This breaks the validator's contract with the loader and is a security hole.

findings.title: Validation accepts allow_implicit_invocation:false from any top-level section, not just root policy
findings.evidence: Merged duplicate from the Security and Data & contracts lenses. The spec says validation passes only if policy.allow_implicit_invocation is boolean false at the document root. The old code checked exactly that: `config.policy?.allow_implicit_invocation===false`. The new code uses `Object.values(config).some(section => section?.allow_implicit_invocation===false)`, so it passes when any top-level section sets the flag to false. Two examples now pass: `{metadata:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}}` with no policy, and `{policy:{allow_implicit_invocation:true}, other:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}}`. The loader reads only config.policy.allow_implicit_invocation, and a missing policy defaults to permitting implicit invocation. So a tool can pass validation as human-only while the loader still lets it be invoked implicitly. This bypasses the authorization control, and the Data & contracts lens notes that it also breaks the validator's contract with the loader.

findings.title: Escape close no longer restores focus to the opening trigger
findings.evidence: The spec says closing with Escape must restore focus to the control that opened it. The before version called state.trigger.focus() after setting state.open=false. The after version only sets state.open=false. Because the renderer unmounts the dialog when state.open is false, the focused element inside the dialog is removed and focus falls back to document.body. Keyboard and screen-reader users lose their place, which breaks the stated contract. The fix is to bring back state.trigger.focus() after state.open=false.
findings.location: module.js: onKey, Escape branch (state.open=false; with the trigger.focus() call removed)

gaps: Not checked at runtime: the exact order in which the renderer unmounts the dialog relative to a synchronous trigger.focus() call, and whether the trigger is still in the DOM and focusable at that moment.

findings.title: Escape close no longer restores focus to the trigger
findings.evidence: The spec says closing with Escape must put focus back on the control that opened the dialog. The before code called state.trigger.focus() after setting state.open=false. The after code drops that call, so onKey only sets state.open=false. The renderer then unmounts the dialog, and the element that had focus goes away with it. Focus ends up on the document body instead of the trigger. This breaks the spec and keyboard/screen-reader accessibility. Per the context, trigger.focus() is the only way to restore focus, and nothing else calls it.

gaps: No tests were supplied, so there may be no regression test checking that focus goes back to the trigger after Escape.

findings.title: Pressing Escape no longer returns focus to the button that opened the dialog
findings.evidence: The spec says closing the dialog with Escape must return focus to the control that opened it. Before the change, the Escape branch of onKey did `state.open=false; state.trigger.focus();`. After the change it only does `state.open=false;`. The context says the renderer removes the dialog when state.open is false, and that trigger.focus() is the available way to restore focus. Nothing else calls trigger.focus(), so the focused element is removed along with the dialog and focus does not go back to the trigger. Keyboard and screen-reader users lose their place, which breaks the spec. Fix: add `state.trigger.focus();` back after `state.open=false;`. This was reported by two reviewers and merged here; the Staff engineer review found the same defect at the same severity (blocker).
findings.location: module.js: onKey, Escape branch — `state.trigger.focus();` was removed after `state.open=false;`

gaps: Not checked at runtime: when the renderer removes the dialog compared with a synchronous trigger.focus() call, and whether the trigger is still on the page and focusable at that moment.
No tests were supplied, so there may be no regression test checking that focus goes back to the trigger after Escape.

findings.title: Selection stored as index; archive resolves it against the current (filtered/reordered) rows, so the wrong row can be archived
findings.evidence: select now returns the index. Per the context, filter and sort replace rows but preserve the selection. archiveSelected then evaluates rows[selection].id against the new rows array, so the same index can point at a different row. That row gets archived, which is a destructive persistence action on the wrong record and violates the spec. If the index is out of range after filtering, rows[selection] is undefined and the code throws a TypeError. The before code stored the immutable unique id at selection time, which was correct. The change reintroduces the bug the spec forbids.

findings.title: No tests cover filter/sort after selection, and no guard for an invalid selection
findings.evidence: The change has no tests for archiving after the rows are filtered or reordered, or for a selection that no longer exists. archiveSelected has no guard for a missing row, so it throws instead of doing nothing or reporting an error.

gaps: Only the diff was supplied, so I could not see the callers or the parent state. I assumed the selection is the value returned by select and is passed back unchanged to archiveSelected.
No test files were supplied, so I could not confirm whether any tests exist.

findings.title: Selection stored as index makes archive act on the wrong row after filter/sort
findings.evidence: Spec requires archive to act on the user-selected row even after filtering or reordering. Context says filter and sort replace rows but preserve selection. The change makes select return the positional index and archiveSelected resolve rows[selection].id against the current rows. After a filter or sort, that index points to a different row, so the wrong item is archived, or rows[selection] is undefined and it throws. The previous code stored the immutable unique id, which was stable across reorders. The change reintroduces the exact bug the spec forbids.

gaps: No tests or UI code supplied to confirm how the parent resets or preserves selection on filter/sort.
Whether the original code's archive(selection) was fully correct depends on callers using the id, which isn't shown.

findings.title: Selection is stored as a row index, so after a filter or sort, archive acts on the wrong row or throws
findings.evidence: Both the Staff engineer and Product reports found this, and I merged them into one finding. After the change, select() returns the position `index` instead of `rows[index].id`. archiveSelected() then calls `archive(rows[selection].id)` on whatever the rows array is at archive time. The context says filter and sort replace rows but keep the selection. So the saved index can point to a different row in the new array, and that row gets archived. Archiving saves the change, so it alters the wrong record and breaks the spec: archive must act on the row the user selected, even after the list is filtered or reordered. If filtering shrinks the list below the saved index, `rows[selection]` is undefined, and reading `.id` throws a TypeError. The before code saved the row's immutable unique id when the user selected it and passed it straight to archive(), so it was correct. The Staff engineer report filed a separate should-fix for the missing guard on an invalid selection. That crash comes from the same index change, so I folded it into this finding.

gaps: The Staff engineer report's should-fix about missing tests for filtering or sorting after a selection is about verification coverage, not a defect the change introduced. No test files were supplied, so I couldn't confirm whether such tests exist. The fix should add a test that archives after the rows are filtered or reordered.

findings.title: Prune predicate widened from exact managed-link match to prefix match, deleting aliases and file links
findings.evidence: The spec defines a managed link as /installed/<name> pointing exactly to /repo/skills/<name>, and says aliases and links to files inside a skill must be kept. The 'before' code checked target==='/repo/skills/'+name. The 'after' code checks target.startsWith('/repo/skills/'). Now any entry not in live is returned for removal if its target is anywhere under /repo/skills/. That includes an alias like 'foo' -> /repo/skills/bar and a file link like 'x' -> /repo/skills/bar/file.md. Because the caller unlinks every name returned, these user-created links get deleted. That is data loss and breaks the contract, and it removes far more than intended. The prefix check also matches siblings such as /repo/skills-old/... only if they start with '/repo/skills/', so that part is fine, but the alias and file-link cases are clearly affected.

gaps: The fixture includes no tests or caller code, so I couldn't check whether the caller backs up or confirms entries before unlinking them, which would decide whether deleted links can be restored.

findings.title: Prune now matches aliases and links to files inside a skill, so the caller deletes links it should keep
findings.evidence: The spec says a managed link must point exactly to /repo/skills/<name> and that aliases and links to files within a skill must be kept. The old check `target==='/repo/skills/'+name` enforced that. The new check `target.startsWith('/repo/skills/')` also matches any non-live alias (e.g. entries {foo:'/repo/skills/bar'}) and any file link (e.g. {x:'/repo/skills/x/README.md'}). prune returns these names and the caller unlinks each one, so links the user wants to keep get removed. The prefix check also matches siblings like '/repo/skills/../other'.

gaps: No tests were supplied. Nothing covers an alias (name differs from the target basename), a link to a file inside a skill, or the exact-match case for a stale managed link.

There is no stated reason for the change, so it's unclear whether it was meant to fix trailing slashes or path normalization. If so, it should match the exact name after normalizing the path, not use a prefix check.

findings.title: Save control no longer activates with Enter or Space
findings.evidence: The old code rendered a native <button>, which the renderer gives built-in keyboard activation. The new code renders a div with role='button' and tabIndex=0, and only an onClick handler. The context says the renderer supplies no keyboard behavior for div, and no onKeyDown or onKeyUp handler is added. The control can still be reached with Tab and clicked with a pointer, but pressing Enter or Space does nothing. This breaks the spec requirement that Save activate with Enter and Space and blocks keyboard-only users from saving.

gaps: I couldn't check visible focus styling or contrast for the div because no CSS or theme was supplied.
I couldn't check whether the renderer handles disabled or loading states for a div used as a button.

findings.title: Save no longer works with Enter or Space, which breaks the keyboard requirement in the spec
findings.evidence: The spec says Save must activate with Enter and Space as well as a pointer click. The before version returned tag:'button', so the renderer's native button keyboard behavior handled both keys. The after version returns tag:'div', role:'button', tabIndex:0 and sets only onClick. According to the context, the renderer gives a div no keyboard behavior and only copies the handlers that are declared, and no onKeyDown/onKeyUp handler is declared. Keyboard users can Tab to Save but can't activate it, so they can't save.

findings.title: Replacing the native button with a div adds no user value and risks a regression
findings.evidence: The before version already met every part of the spec with a native button (type:'button', and there is no form to worry about). Changing it to a div with role='button' gives users nothing new, and to get back to equal behavior the keyboard handling has to be rebuilt by hand. Keep tag:'button'.

There's no explanation of why the change was made, so I couldn't check whether a design need justified using a div.

findings.title: Transaction boundary removed; a rejected credit leaves the debit committed (partial transfer / data loss)
findings.evidence: The spec says to use the supplied transaction boundary so all writes commit together, and a rejected debit must leave both balances unchanged. The new code calls db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount) and then db.save(to, ...) directly. According to the context, db.save writes immediately and throws for a frozen destination account. So if 'to' is frozen, the debit to 'from' is already saved and is never rolled back, and the funds are lost. The old code wrapped both writes in db.transaction(tx => ...), which commits only if the callback returns.
findings.location: module.js transfer(): lines `db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount);` and `db.save(to, db.get(to)+amount);`

findings.title: Reads and writes moved outside the isolated snapshot, so concurrent transfers can lose updates
findings.evidence: The new code reads with db.get and then writes with db.save outside any transaction. Two transfers running at the same time can read the same balance, and one overwrites the other's update. Before, tx.get/tx.save ran against an isolated snapshot.

findings.title: Return value of the transaction is no longer propagated
findings.evidence: Before, the function returned db.transaction(...), so callers could await it or observe the commit result. After, transfer returns undefined. That is a contract change for any caller that depends on the returned value.

gaps: No tests were supplied. Nothing covers the case where the destination is frozen or the transfer is rejected, which should check that both balances are unchanged.
The callers of transfer() weren't supplied, so I couldn't confirm whether any of them use the return value.

findings.title: Transaction boundary removed; a failed credit leaves the debit committed, so money is lost
findings.evidence: The spec says a rejected debit must leave both balances unchanged and all writes must commit together. The context says db.save writes immediately and throws when the destination account is frozen. In the new code, db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount) commits first. If db.save(to, ...) then throws for a frozen destination, the source has already been debited and the destination never gets the credit, so the amount is lost. The previous code used db.transaction(tx => ...), which writes to an isolated snapshot and commits only if the callback returns, so both writes either applied together or not at all.

findings.title: Transaction boundary removed: a frozen destination leaves the source debited (partial failure, lost funds)

If the second db.save(to, ...) throws because the destination account is frozen, the debit from the first db.save(from, db.get(from)-amount) is already persisted and nothing rolls it back. That breaks the spec: 'A rejected debit must leave both balances unchanged... all writes commit together.' The before version used db.transaction, which commits only if the callback returns.

Without the transaction there is no idempotency key and no atomic commit, so remediation needs manual balance reconciliation. Nothing in the code records which leg succeeded.

With no caller backup, this causes data loss and returns true where the spec requires preserving the target and returning false.

findings.title: Preserve real files and directories at installation targets
findings.evidence: The unconditional deletion and replacement remove existing file or directory nodes, including user-created directory content, with no backup. The function then returns true instead of the required false for these conflicts. Restore the non-link guard before modifying the target.

findings.title: Retries use a new idempotency key and can create duplicate charges
findings.evidence: The change replaces charge(event.id) with charge(attemptId). Retries retain event.id but receive a new attemptId, so the provider cannot reuse the existing charge. A retry, including after a worker restart, can create a second charge, violating the specification. Restore event.id as the idempotency key.

findings.title: Preserve the event ID as the charge idempotency key
findings.evidence: The change replaces charge(event.id) with charge(attemptId). Retries retain event.id but receive a new attemptId, so the provider no longer deduplicates them and can create a second charge, violating the retry contract, including after worker restarts.

findings.title: Retries can create duplicate charges
findings.evidence: Replacing charge(event.id) with charge(attemptId) changes the provider idempotency key on every retry: event.id remains the same, but attemptId is new. Retries, including after worker restarts, can therefore create a second charge, violating the specification. Restore event.id as the key. This merges matching findings from Operability and Staff engineer.

findings.title: The /repo check now looks at only one alias hop, so a longer link chain can write into /repo
findings.evidence: The change replaced `const resolved=canonical(path,links)` with `const resolved=links[path] || path`, so the guard now follows a single alias. The write still goes to `canonical(path,links)+'/tool'`, which follows the whole chain. Example: links={'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}. install('/a') checks '/b', which passes the guard, and then records the operation '/repo/x/tool'. The spec requires refusing any destination that resolves anywhere inside /repo before an operation is recorded. That contract is now broken, and an install can write into the protected tree.

findings.title: Guard now checks only one hop of the link chain, so multi-hop aliases into /repo get through
findings.evidence: The after code sets resolved=links[path] || path, which follows only a single alias. The push still uses canonical(path,links), which follows the whole chain. Example: links={'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}. Then resolved='/b', the check passes, and the code records '/repo/x/tool'. The caller then writes into /repo. The spec says to refuse any destination that resolves within /repo before an operation is recorded, so this is a security hole and a broken contract. The before code checked canonical(path,links), which was correct.

findings.title: The checked path and the written path are computed differently
findings.evidence: The guard checks one value (a single-hop lookup) and the push writes a different one (canonical(...)). Compute canonical once, check it, and push that same value. Then the check always matches the write.

gaps: No tests were supplied. I couldn't confirm coverage for multi-hop chains that end inside /repo, for '/repo' exactly, or for look-alike prefixes such as '/repository'.
Cyclic links would make canonical loop forever. This was already true before the change and the context doesn't say whether cycles can occur.

findings.title: The /repo guard follows only one alias hop, but the write follows the whole chain, so multi-hop links can write into /repo
findings.evidence: Infrastructure and Staff engineer both reported this; they are merged here. The change replaced `const resolved=canonical(path,links)` with `const resolved=links[path] || path`, so the guard now follows a single alias. The write still uses `canonical(path,links)+'/tool'`, which follows the full chain. Example: with links={'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}, install('/a') checks '/b', passes the guard, and records '/repo/x/tool'. The caller then writes into that physical destination inside /repo. This breaks the spec: a destination that resolves anywhere within /repo must be refused before any operation is recorded. It is a security hole and a broken contract. Staff engineer also filed a should-fix because the checked value and the written value come from different calculations. That has the same root cause, so it is merged here. Fix: compute canonical(path,links) once, check that value, and push the same value.

gaps: No tests were supplied. Coverage is unconfirmed for multi-hop chains that end inside /repo, for '/repo' exactly, and for look-alike prefixes such as '/repository'.
Cyclic links would make canonical loop forever. This was already true before the change and is not a defect the change introduced. The context doesn't say whether cycles can occur.

findings.title: Prune predicate widened from exact managed-link match to prefix match, deleting aliases and intra-skill file links
findings.evidence: The spec says a managed link must point exactly to /repo/skills/<name>, and aliases and links to files within a skill must be kept. The before code checked target==='/repo/skills/'+name. The after code checks target.startsWith('/repo/skills/'). Now any non-live entry whose target is anywhere under /repo/skills/ is returned. Two examples: an alias foo -> /repo/skills/bar, and a file link x -> /repo/skills/bar/file.md. The caller unlinks every returned name, so user-created aliases and file links get deleted. This is data loss and goes beyond the stated managed-link scope.

gaps: No tests or fixtures were provided that cover aliases or links to files within a skill, so the regression is inferred from the spec and the code rather than observed in a run.
Path normalisation (trailing slashes, symlink resolution) of entries targets isn't specified, so exact-match edge cases weren't checked.

findings.title: Prune now removes aliases and links into files within a skill
findings.evidence: The spec says to prune only managed links where /installed/<name> points exactly to /repo/skills/<name>, and to keep aliases and links to files within a skill. The old check `target==='/repo/skills/'+name` did this. The new check `target.startsWith('/repo/skills/')` also matches aliases (e.g. name 'foo' -> '/repo/skills/bar') and file links (e.g. 'x' -> '/repo/skills/bar/README.md'). If such a name is not in live, prune returns it and the caller unlinks it. That deletes links the user wanted to keep.

findings.title: Prefix match also accepts lookalike or non-normalized paths
findings.evidence: `startsWith('/repo/skills/')` also matches targets like '/repo/skills/../other' or '/repo/skills/' with an empty name. It does not check that the name matches the target, so links that are not managed can be pruned.

gaps: No tests were supplied. Nothing checks that aliases, links to files within a skill, and exact managed links behave correctly under the new predicate.

findings.title: Prune predicate widened from an exact managed-link match to a prefix match, so aliases and links to files within a skill get deleted
findings.evidence: Infrastructure and Staff engineer both reported this blocker; this entry merges their reports. The spec says to prune only managed links, where /installed/<name> points exactly to /repo/skills/<name>, and to keep aliases and links to files within a skill. The before code checked `target==='/repo/skills/'+name`, which matches that rule. The after code checks only `target.startsWith('/repo/skills/')` and no longer checks that the target matches the name. Any entry that is not in `live` and points anywhere under /repo/skills/ is now returned. Examples: an alias foo -> /repo/skills/bar, and a file link x -> /repo/skills/bar/README.md. The context says the caller unlinks every returned name, so links the user wanted to keep are deleted. This is data loss. Staff engineer filed a separate should-fix about lookalike or non-normalized targets such as '/repo/skills/../other' and the bare '/repo/skills/'. Those have the same cause (the prefix match with no name check), so they are folded into this finding rather than kept as a separate defect.

gaps: No tests or fixtures were supplied for aliases, links to files within a skill, or exact managed links. The regression is inferred from the spec and the code, not seen in a run.
The spec doesn't say how targets in entries are normalized (trailing slashes, '..' segments, symlink resolution), so edge cases of the exact match weren't checked.

I found no security defects in this change. I checked it by reading the code side by side; I didn't run any tests. Both versions return null for a missing session, an inactive member, a missing row or a tenant mismatch. In both, when the row is missing, `row?.tenant===session.tenant ? row : null` returns null either way.

One edge case existed before this change and still does: if both `session.tenant` and `row.tenant` are undefined, the tenant check passes. The fixture context doesn't say whether trusted middleware always sets `session.tenant` for active members, so I couldn't confirm this case is ruled out.

findings.title: Refactor loses the explicit `!row` guard, so a missing row can leak `undefined` instead of `null`
findings.evidence: The before code returned null whenever `!row`. The after code returns `row` whenever `row?.tenant === session.tenant`. If `find` returns `undefined` and `session.tenant` is `undefined`, both sides are `undefined`. The function then returns `undefined`, not `null`. The context says tenant IDs are opaque strings and the middleware is trusted, so this is unlikely in practice. It is still a narrow change from the old contract. The spec only promises null for unauthenticated callers, so this is not a spec violation.

findings.title: No tests accompany the behavior-preserving refactor
findings.evidence: The change rewrites the auth and tenant guards with optional chaining, and no tests are supplied. Cases worth pinning: null or undefined session, `active` false or truthy-but-not-true, `find` returning null or undefined, a tenant mismatch, and a tenant match.

gaps: No test suite was supplied, so I could not check coverage of the null-session, inactive-session, missing-row and tenant-mismatch cases.
Whether callers depend on a strict `null` return, rather than any falsy value, is not visible in the fixture.

I compared the before and after code by reading them; I didn't run anything. Given the stated constraints, they behave the same. A null or undefined session returns null. So does `active` set to anything other than `true`. A null or undefined row from `find` gives `row?.tenant` as undefined, which never equals a string tenant ID, so that also returns null. A tenant mismatch returns null, and a tenant match returns the row.

I removed the Staff engineer finding that a missing row could return `undefined` instead of `null`. It only happens if `session.tenant` is undefined for an active member, but the context says tenant IDs are opaque strings and sessions come from trusted middleware. The same undefined-tenant case also existed before this change; the Security report noted it as an existing gap, not a new defect.

I removed the Staff engineer finding about missing tests. No tests is not a defect introduced by this change, and the change keeps the same behavior. I'm recording it here as a gap instead: no test suite was supplied, so tests for the null session, inactive session, missing row, mismatched tenant and matching tenant cases couldn't be checked.

The fixture doesn't show whether callers depend on a strict `null` return rather than any falsy value. Under the stated constraints, though, the after code never returns anything other than null or the matching row.

findings.title: Selection now stores a row position instead of the row id, so archive can hit the wrong row after a filter or sort
findings.evidence: In the after code, select returns `index` and archiveSelected calls `archive(rows[selection].id)`. Per the context, filter and sort replace `rows` but keep the stored selection. After a filter or sort, `rows[selection]` can be a different row from the one the user picked, so the wrong row gets archived and persisted (data loss). If the filtered list is shorter than the stored index, `rows[selection]` is undefined and reading `.id` throws. The spec says archive must act on the selected row even after filtering or reordering. The before code stored the immutable unique id, which met that requirement.

findings.title: No test covers archiving after the list is filtered or reordered
findings.evidence: The spec specifically requires correct behaviour when the list is filtered or reordered after selection. The change has no test that selects a row, filters or sorts the rows, then checks that archive is called with the original id. A test like that would catch this regression.

gaps: No test files were supplied, so I couldn't confirm what tests exist.
I couldn't confirm whether any other callers depend on select returning an id.

findings.title: Archive hits the wrong row after the list is filtered or re-sorted
findings.evidence: The spec says archive must act on the row the user selected, even if the list is filtered or reordered after selection. The context says filter and sort replace `rows` but keep the selection. The change makes `select` return `index` (a position) instead of `rows[index].id`, and `archiveSelected` now calls `archive(rows[selection].id)`. Once rows are filtered or re-sorted, that stored position points to a different row. So the wrong record gets archived (persisted data loss), or it fails with a TypeError if the index is now past the end of the list. Before the change, the code stored the row's immutable unique id and passed it straight to `archive`, which met the spec.

findings.title: Selection now stores a row position instead of the row id, so archive can hit the wrong row after a filter or sort
findings.evidence: In the after code, `select` returns `index` instead of `rows[index].id`, and `archiveSelected` calls `archive(rows[selection].id)`. The context says filter and sort replace `rows` but keep the stored selection. After a filter or sort, `rows[selection]` can be a different row from the one the user picked. That row's id is then passed to `archive`, the persistence callback, so the wrong record is archived (persisted data loss). If the new `rows` is shorter than the stored index, `rows[selection]` is undefined and reading `.id` throws a TypeError. This breaks the spec, which says archive must act on the selected row even after filtering or reordering. The before code stored the immutable unique id and passed it straight to `archive`, which met the spec. The Product lens reported the same defect at the same severity, so the two reports are merged here.

findings.title: Retries use a new idempotency key and can create duplicate charges
findings.evidence: The change passes attemptId to charge instead of event.id. A retry retains event.id but receives a new attemptId, so the provider cannot return the existing charge using its equal-key guarantee. This violates the requirement that retries, including after worker restarts, must not create a second charge. Restore event.id as the key.

findings.title: Preserve the event ID as the charge idempotency key
findings.evidence: The change passes attemptId to charge(), but retries of the same event receive new attemptId values. The provider therefore receives different keys and can create a second charge, violating the retry guarantee. Using event.id preserves idempotency across retries and worker restarts.

findings.title: Retries can create duplicate charges
findings.evidence: charge(attemptId) replaces the stable event.id with a key that changes on retry. The provider's equal-key idempotency guarantee therefore no longer prevents a second charge, violating the retry contract, including after worker restarts. Merged corroborating finding from Staff engineer; restore event.id as the key.

findings.title: Off-by-one in retry guard allows a fourth attempt, which breaks the three-attempt limit
findings.evidence: The spec says to retry at most three total attempts, and attempts start at 1. The guard was changed from `attempt<3` to `attempt<=3`. If attempt 3 returns retryable, the new guard (3<=3) is true, so the code calls `send(request, 4)` and `request(4)` runs. That is four total attempts. The function also returns attempt 4's response, not the third attempt's response as the spec's "return the last response" requires. The old guard (`attempt<3`) stopped after attempt 3 and returned its result, which matched the spec.

gaps: The change came without tests, so nothing checks the attempt limit. There should be a test where every response is retryable that asserts request is called exactly 3 times and the third response is returned, plus one where success on the first attempt returns immediately.

findings.title: Off-by-one retry bound makes up to four total attempts instead of three
findings.evidence: The retry guard changed from `attempt<3` to `attempt<=3`. Attempts start at 1, so if attempts 1, 2 and 3 all return `retryable`, the check `3<=3` passes and `send` calls `request(4)`. That is a fourth attempt, which breaks the spec's limit of "at most three total attempts". During a transient outage, every caller now sends about 33% more load to a dependency that is already failing. Because the extra attempt is repeated, the response returned is from attempt 4, not attempt 3. If `request` is not idempotent, the extra attempt also adds one more duplicate side effect. The old guard `attempt<3` capped calls at exactly three.
findings.location: module.js: send(), line `if(result.retryable && attempt<=3) return send(request, attempt+1);`

gaps: The fixture doesn't say whether request(attempt) is idempotent, so I couldn't measure the side-effect impact of the extra fourth attempt.
There's no logging or metrics around retries before or after the change, so I couldn't check whether on-call can see retry exhaustion. This gap existed before the change.

findings.title: Off-by-one in the retry guard allows a fourth attempt, breaking the three-attempt limit
findings.evidence: Both the Staff engineer and Operability lenses reported this; the two reports are merged here. The spec says to retry at most three total attempts and to return the last response. Attempts start at 1. The guard changed from `attempt<3` to `attempt<=3`. If attempts 1, 2 and 3 are all retryable, then at attempt 3 the check `3<=3` is true, so `send(request, 4)` runs `request(4)`. That is four total attempts, and the function returns attempt 4's response. The old guard stopped after attempt 3 and returned its result, which matched the spec. Success still returns immediately because `retryable` is false. The Operability lens added a supported consequence: during a transient outage, each exhausted call now sends about 33% more load to a dependency that is already failing. The extra attempt may also repeat side effects, but that depends on whether `request` is idempotent, which the fixture doesn't say.
findings.location: module.js: send(), line 3 `if(result.retryable && attempt<=3) return send(request, attempt+1);`

gaps: The change has no tests. One test should make every response retryable and assert that `request` is called exactly 3 times and the third response is returned. Another should check that success on the first attempt returns immediately.
The fixture doesn't say whether `request(attempt)` is idempotent, so I couldn't confirm the duplicate side effect from the extra attempt.
Retries have no logging or metrics. This was already true before the change, so it isn't counted as an introduced defect.

findings.title: Removing `name` from the response breaks installed mobile clients that still use it
findings.evidence: Before: `return {id:row.id, name:row.name, displayName:row.name}`. After: `return {id:row.id, displayName:row.name}`. The spec says installed clients that still read `name` must keep working, and every consumer must keep showing a label. Mobile releases stay active for 90 days, and the legacy code calls `payload.name.toUpperCase()`. With `name` gone, `payload.name` is undefined, so that call throws a TypeError and those clients stop showing the label. This is a user-facing break and breaks the API contract. Fix: keep `name: row.name` next to `displayName` until the 90-day mobile support window has passed.

findings.title: Removing `name` breaks installed mobile clients that still read payload.name

The after version returns only {id, displayName}, so payload.name is now undefined and the legacy call throws a TypeError. Those clients can't render a label, which breaks the API contract for users. Fix: keep `name: row.name` next to `displayName` until the 90-day deprecation window ends.

findings.title: The /repo guard checks only one link hop, but the write goes to the end of the full link chain
findings.evidence: The after version sets `resolved=links[path] || path`, so the check only looks one link deep. The write still goes to `canonical(path,links)+'/tool'`, which follows every link to the end. With links {'/a':'/b','/b':'/repo/x'}, install('/a') checks '/b', which passes. It then records '/repo/x/tool', so a write lands inside /repo. The before version checked the full canonical path, which is the same path it writes to. The spec says any destination that resolves within /repo must be refused before an operation is recorded, so this change breaks that guarantee and lets writes reach protected paths.

gaps: Didn't check how canonical() behaves when links form a cycle. The code didn't change there, and the brief says links are absolute directory aliases.

findings.title: The guard checks only one link hop, so a chain of links can still reach /repo

That breaks the spec rule to refuse any destination that ends up inside /repo before an operation is recorded. The old code checked the canonical path, so this is a regression and a security hole.

findings.title: The path that gets checked is not the path that gets written
findings.evidence: The check uses one value (resolved) and the push works out the path again with canonical(). The two are computed differently, so they can disagree. Work out the canonical path once and use that same value for both the check and the push (`operations.push(resolved+'/tool')`).

gaps: The change includes no tests. Add a regression test where a chain of two or more links ends in /repo or /repo/sub, and check that it returns false and leaves operations empty.

findings.title: Tenant authorization check now trusts the tenant value from the request instead of the session
findings.evidence: The change swaps `row.tenant === session.tenant` for `row.tenant === request.tenant`. The context says find(id) is a global lookup with no tenant scoping and that request parameters come straight from the URL. That means any authenticated user can read any tenant's document by putting the document's tenant in the request (e.g. ?id=X&tenant=victimTenant). This breaks the spec rule that a document is returned only to a session from the document's tenant and that request tenant filters are untrusted. It is an IDOR/cross-tenant data exposure. Fix: compare against the verified `session.tenant`, as the code did before.
findings.location: module.js:read, line 3 (`return row && row.tenant === request.tenant ? row : null;`)

findings.title: Tenant authorization now trusts the request tenant instead of the verified session tenant, allowing cross-tenant document reads
findings.evidence: Before: `row.tenant === session.tenant`. After: `row.tenant === request.tenant`. The spec says a document may be returned only to a session from the document's tenant, and that request tenant filters are untrusted. The context says request parameters come straight from the URL and find(id) is a global lookup with no tenant scoping, so this comparison is the only tenant check. Any authenticated caller can read any tenant's document by sending a request like ?id=X&tenant=<victimTenant>. That is cross-tenant data exposure (IDOR). The session is no longer used for authorization. Fix: compare against session.tenant again. Merged duplicate: the Staff engineer lens reported the same blocker with the same reasoning.
