findings.title: Off-by-one allows four total attempts, violating the three-attempt cap
findings.evidence: The spec says to retry for at most three total attempts. The change from `attempt<3` to `attempt<=3` means that when attempt 3 returns a retryable result, send calls request(4). That makes four total attempts for a persistently transient failure. The original `attempt<3` condition stopped at three. The change introduces the bug.

It should assert exactly three calls and that the third response is returned. It should also assert that success on attempt 1 or 2 returns immediately. A test like that would have caught the fourth-attempt regression.

findings.title: Off-by-one allows four attempts, exceeding the three-attempt retry cap
findings.evidence: Spec: at most three total attempts. Attempts start at 1. With `attempt<=3`, a retryable result at attempt 3 triggers send(request, 4), so request is called a fourth time. The before code (`attempt<3`) correctly capped at 3. Under a sustained transient failure this adds an extra call to the downstream dependency, which is a non-idempotent side-effect risk (e.g. duplicate writes) and extra load during an outage. It also makes observed attempt counts disagree with the documented limit, which misleads on-call triage.

findings.title: No visibility into retries or final failure
findings.evidence: The retry loop emits no log, metric, or attempt/status context. The last retryable result is returned silently, so on-call cannot tell that retries were exhausted or how many attempts were made. There is also no backoff or timeout, though the synchronous contract limits what can be done here.

gaps: The idempotency of request(attempt) is unknown, so the severity of the extra fourth call depends on whether the operation has side effects.
No tests were supplied to show whether attempt counts are verified.
No information on callers' own retry layers, which could multiply the extra attempt.

findings.title: Off-by-one allows four total attempts, violating the three-attempt cap

findings.title: Stale-response guard removed; out-of-order responses overwrite newer results
findings.evidence: The before version saved `const request=++state.request` and skipped the update when `request!==state.request`. The after version still increments state.request but never checks it, and the callback always runs `state.items=items`. The context says fetchResults does not guarantee callback order, so an older query's response can arrive last and replace the newest query's results. That breaks the spec: 'must display results for the most recently entered query.'

findings.title: Stale-response guard removed: older search results can overwrite newer query results
findings.evidence: Before: `const request=++state.request;` and the callback checked `if(request!==state.request) return;`, so only the latest request could update the results. After: `++state.request;` still runs, but the callback always sets `state.items=items;` with no check. The context says fetchResults does not guarantee callback order and the input handler calls search for every query, so a slow response for an earlier query (e.g. 'ca') that arrives after the response for 'cat' will replace the results. The screen then shows results for an older query, which breaks the spec requirement to show results for the most recent query. Users see results that don't match what they typed.

gaps: No rendering code, markup, or loading/error/empty-state handling was provided, so keyboard operability, semantics, focus, contrast, and responsive behavior could not be checked.
Can't tell whether screen-reader announcements of result updates (e.g. live regions) would also announce stale results.

findings.title: Stale-response guard removed, so an older query's results can replace the newest query's results

findings.title: Removed conflict guard: install deletes and overwrites real directories and files, losing data with no rollback path
findings.evidence: Before: `if(fs[target] && fs[target].kind!=='link') return false;` kept non-link nodes. After: `delete fs[target]; fs[target]={kind:'link',to:source}; return true;` runs with no check. Any existing directory node (which may hold user-created content) or file node gets replaced by a link. The context says assignment replaces the whole node and callers keep no backup, so the content is lost for good. This breaks the spec, which says to keep real directories and files and return false on those conflicts. It also makes the damage much wider: any target path can be overwritten.

findings.title: Validation accepts allow_implicit_invocation:false from any top-level section, not just policy
findings.evidence: The spec says validation passes only if policy.allow_implicit_invocation is boolean false at the document root. The new code, `Object.values(config).some(section => section?.allow_implicit_invocation===false)`, passes if any top-level section has that value. Example: `{ other: { allow_implicit_invocation: false } }` with no policy block now passes. But the loader reads only config.policy.allow_implicit_invocation, and a missing policy means implicit invocation is allowed. So a config can pass as human-only while the loader still lets it be invoked implicitly. The same happens with `{ policy: { allow_implicit_invocation: true }, x: { allow_implicit_invocation: false } }`. This turns the old deny-by-default check into a fail-open one and lets the human-only restriction be bypassed.

Example: a config like `{metadata:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}}` with no policy now validates. The loader reads only `config.policy.allow_implicit_invocation`, and a missing policy means implicit invocation is allowed. So a tool that should be human-only can pass validation and still be invoked implicitly. The same happens when policy.allow_implicit_invocation is true and another section has false. This breaks the validation contract and is a security hole. The old check, `config.policy?.allow_implicit_invocation===false`, was correct.

findings.title: Off-by-one retry bound allows four total attempts instead of three
findings.evidence: The guard changed from `attempt<3` to `attempt<=3`. Attempts start at 1. When attempt 3 returns a retryable response, `3<=3` is true, so `send` recurses and calls `request(4)`. A transient failure now gets 4 total attempts, but the spec says "retry at most three total attempts, then return the last response". This breaks the retry contract and adds 33% more load on a dependency that is already failing, which can make an outage worse. In the context, a directory node can hold user-created content, assignment replaces the whole node, and callers keep no backup. So any directory or file at the target is destroyed with no way to roll it back, and the function returns true when the contract says it should return false.

findings.title: Prune check widened from exact managed-link match to prefix match, so aliases and in-skill file links get deleted
findings.evidence: The spec says a link counts as managed only when /installed/<name> points exactly to /repo/skills/<name>, and that aliases and links to files inside a skill must be kept. The before code checked target==='/repo/skills/'+name. The after code checks target.startsWith('/repo/skills/'). Any entry not in live whose target is anywhere under /repo/skills/ is now returned, for example an alias foo -> /repo/skills/bar or a file link x -> /repo/skills/bar/file.md. The caller unlinks every returned name, so these links are removed and user installs are lost. The prefix check also matches siblings such as /repo/skills-old/... because there is no trailing boundary beyond the slash, and it doesn't normalise paths like /repo/skills/../other. This increases how many links a single prune can delete, and the change gives no dry-run or rollback path for removed links.

gaps: No tests or caller code were supplied, so I couldn't confirm whether the caller has a dry-run or confirmation step before unlinking.
Whether targets are normalised before prune receives them is unspecified, so path traversal through '..' segments wasn't verified.

findings.title: Prefix match prunes aliases and links to files within a skill, which the spec says to keep
findings.evidence: The old check `target==='/repo/skills/'+name` only matched links whose name matches the target directory. The new check `target.startsWith('/repo/skills/')` matches any target under the skills root. So an alias such as `foo -> /repo/skills/bar`, or a link into a skill's files such as `foo -> /repo/skills/foo/README.md`, is now returned whenever `foo` is not in `live`. The caller unlinks every returned entry, so user-created aliases and file links get deleted. The spec says to preserve both.

findings.title: Prefix check matches sibling paths and non-normalized targets
findings.evidence: `startsWith('/repo/skills/')` also matches unnormalized targets like `/repo/skills/../other` and `/repo/skills//foo`. These resolve outside the skills tree or don't match the exact managed form, so links outside the managed set can be removed. The old exact-equality check could not do this.
